::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="foundations probability events" data-difficulty="0" #q-foundations-events}
## Question 1: Events: at least one, exactly one, or neither

For a randomly selected student, let $A$ be the event that they attend a revision
session and $B$ the event that they complete a practice paper. Suppose
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(A)=0.60,\qquad \mathrm{Pr}(B)=0.45,\qquad
\mathrm{Pr}(A\cap B)=0.25.
$$

(a) Find the probability that the student does at least one of these activities.  
(b) Find the probability that they do neither activity.  
(c) Find the probability that they do exactly one activity. Explain why this
differs from part (a).

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Inclusion–exclusion gives
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(A\cup B)=0.60+0.45-0.25=0.80.
$$
The union includes students who do both activities.

**(b)** Neither activity is the complement of the union, so its probability is
$1-0.80=0.20$.

**(c)** The two disjoint possibilities are attending only and completing only:
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(A\cap B^c)+\mathrm{Pr}(A^c\cap B)
=(0.60-0.25)+(0.45-0.25)=0.55.
$$
Exactly one excludes the intersection. As a check, the four probabilities for
attending only, completing only, both, and neither sum to
$0.35+0.20+0.25+0.20=1$.

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="foundations probability conditional-probability" data-difficulty="0" #q-foundations-conditional-table}
## Question 2: Conditional probabilities from a two-way table

A group of $100$ students is classified as follows. Select one student uniformly
at random. Let $R$ mean that they used a revision resource and $P$ that they
passed a short quiz.

| Resource use | Passed | Did not pass | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Used the resource | 36 | 24 | 60 |
| Did not use the resource | 14 | 26 | 40 |
| Total | 50 | 50 | 100 |

(a) Find $\mathrm{Pr}(R\cap P)$ and $\mathrm{Pr}(P)$.  
(b) Find $\mathrm{Pr}(P\mid R)$ and $\mathrm{Pr}(R\mid P)$.  
(c) Are $R$ and $P$ independent? Does the table establish that using the resource
causes a higher chance of passing?

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Both probabilities use all $100$ students as the denominator:
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(R\cap P)=\frac{36}{100}=0.36,\qquad
\mathrm{Pr}(P)=\frac{50}{100}=0.50.
$$

**(b)** Conditioning changes the group over which we calculate the proportion:
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(P\mid R)=\frac{36}{60}=0.60,\qquad
\mathrm{Pr}(R\mid P)=\frac{36}{50}=0.72.
$$
Reversing the conditioning does not generally give the same probability.

**(c)** They are not independent because $\mathrm{Pr}(P\mid R)=0.60$ differs
from $\mathrm{Pr}(P)=0.50$. Equivalently, $0.36\ne(0.60)(0.50)$.
This is an association in the group. The table alone does not establish
causation; for example, students who chose the resource might also have spent
more time revising.

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="foundations probability conditional-probability independence" data-difficulty="1" #q-foundations-without-replacement}
## Question 3: Sampling without replacement

A bag contains $3$ red counters and $2$ blue counters. Two counters are drawn
uniformly at random, one after the other, **without replacement**. Let $R_1$
and $R_2$ denote a red counter on the first and second draws respectively.

(a) Find $\mathrm{Pr}(R_1\cap R_2)$.  
(b) Find the probability of exactly one red counter.  
(c) Use the law of total probability to find $\mathrm{Pr}(R_2)$. Are $R_1$
and $R_2$ independent?

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** After drawing one red counter, $2$ of the remaining $4$ counters are red:
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(R_1\cap R_2)
=\mathrm{Pr}(R_1)\mathrm{Pr}(R_2\mid R_1)
=\frac35\frac24=\frac3{10}.
$$

**(b)** Red then blue and blue then red are disjoint outcomes, giving
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(\text{exactly one red})
=\frac35\frac24+\frac25\frac34=\frac35.
$$

**(c)** Partitioning by the colour of the first counter,
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(R_2)
=\frac35\frac24+\frac25\frac34=\frac35.
$$
The marginal red probability is the same on each draw, but
$\mathrm{Pr}(R_2\mid R_1)=1/2\ne3/5$. The draws are dependent.
Equal marginal distributions do not imply independence, and multiplying
$(3/5)(3/5)$ would give the wrong answer to part (a).

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="foundations probability events independence" data-difficulty="0" #q-foundations-independent-disjoint}
## Question 4: Independent or mutually exclusive?

Roll a fair six-sided die. Define
$$
A=\{2,4,6\},\qquad B=\{1,2,3,4\},\qquad C=\{1,3,5\}.
$$

(a) Show that $A$ and $B$ are independent. Are they mutually exclusive?  
(b) Are $A$ and $C$ mutually exclusive, exhaustive, or independent?  
(c) Can two events of positive probability be both independent and mutually
exclusive? Justify your answer.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Since $A\cap B=\{2,4\}$,
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(A\cap B)=\frac26=\frac13
=\frac12\frac23=\mathrm{Pr}(A)\mathrm{Pr}(B).
$$
They are independent but not mutually exclusive: both occur on outcomes $2$
and $4$.

**(b)** The events $A$ and $C$ are mutually exclusive and exhaustive: exactly
one occurs on every roll. They are not independent because
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(A\cap C)=0\ne\frac14
=\mathrm{Pr}(A)\mathrm{Pr}(C).
$$

**(c)** No. Mutual exclusivity requires an intersection of probability zero,
whereas independence of two positive-probability events requires a strictly
positive intersection probability. Knowing one such disjoint event occurred
rules out the other.

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="foundations probability conditional-probability total-probability bayes" data-difficulty="1" #q-foundations-total-probability}
## Question 5: Total probability across three suppliers

A shop obtains $50\%$ of its items from supplier $A$, $30\%$ from $B$, and
$20\%$ from $C$. Their respective defect probabilities are $0.02$, $0.04$,
and $0.05$. Select one item uniformly at random from the shop's stock, and let
$D$ denote a defect.

(a) Find $\mathrm{Pr}(D)$. Explain why simply averaging the three defect
probabilities is inappropriate.  
(b) Given that the item is defective, find the probability that it came from
supplier $C$.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Supplier identity partitions the stock, so
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(D)
=(0.50)(0.02)+(0.30)(0.04)+(0.20)(0.05)=0.032.
$$
The rates need weights equal to the suppliers' shares of the stock. An
unweighted average would instead describe equal shares from all three suppliers.

**(b)** Bayes' theorem gives
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(C\mid D)
=\frac{\mathrm{Pr}(D\mid C)\mathrm{Pr}(C)}{\mathrm{Pr}(D)}
=\frac{(0.05)(0.20)}{0.032}=\frac5{16}=0.3125.
$$
Supplier $C$ accounts for $20\%$ of all items but $31.25\%$ of defective items.

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="foundations probability conditional-probability bayes" data-difficulty="1" #q-foundations-bayes-alarm}
## Question 6: Bayes' theorem and a rare fault

A fault is present in $1\%$ of components. An automated check flags $90\%$ of
faulty components, but also flags $5\%$ of components without a fault. Let $F$
denote a fault and $A$ a flag.

(a) Find the probability that a component is flagged.  
(b) Find $\mathrm{Pr}(F\mid A)$. Explain why it is not $0.90$.  
(c) Check your answer using the expected numbers of faulty and non-faulty
flagged components in a batch of $10{,}000$.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** By total probability,
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(A)=(0.90)(0.01)+(0.05)(0.99)=0.0585.
$$

**(b)** Bayes' theorem gives
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(F\mid A)=\frac{(0.90)(0.01)}{0.0585}
=\frac2{13}\approx0.1538.
$$
The value $0.90$ is $\mathrm{Pr}(A\mid F)$, the probability of a flag given a
fault. Here we need the reverse conditioning. Most components have no fault,
so false flags can outnumber true flags despite a relatively small false-flag rate.

**(c)** The expected numbers are $100$ faulty and $9{,}900$ non-faulty components.
Of these, $90$ and $495$, respectively, are expected to be flagged. The ratio
$90/(90+495)=2/13$ agrees with part (b). These are expected counts, not a claim
that every batch has exactly those counts.

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="foundations probability pmf cdf expectation variance" data-difficulty="1" #q-foundations-discrete-distribution}
## Question 7: A discrete distribution from probabilities to moments

A random variable $X$ has probability mass function
$$
p_X(x)=c(x+1),\qquad x\in\{0,1,2,3\},
$$
and zero probability elsewhere.

(a) Find $c$.  
(b) Write the full cumulative distribution function $F_X(x)$.  
(c) Find $\mathrm{Pr}(1<X\le3)$ and $\mathrm{Pr}(1\le X\le3)$.  
(d) Find $\mathrm{E}[X]$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)$.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** The probabilities must sum to one: $c(1+2+3+4)=1$, so $c=1/10$.

**(b)** The CDF includes all probability at or below its argument:
$$
F_X(x)=
\begin{cases}
0,&x<0,\\
0.1,&0\le x<1,\\
0.3,&1\le x<2,\\
0.6,&2\le x<3,\\
1,&x\ge3.
\end{cases}
$$
It is right-continuous, with a jump of size $p_X(x)$ at each support point.

**(c)** We have
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(1<X\le3)=0.3+0.4=0.7,
\qquad
\mathrm{Pr}(1\le X\le3)=0.2+0.3+0.4=0.9.
$$
Equivalently, the first is $F_X(3)-F_X(1)$. Including the lower endpoint adds
the probability mass $\mathrm{Pr}(X=1)=0.2$.

**(d)** The first two moments are
$$
\mathrm{E}[X]=\frac{0+2+6+12}{10}=2,\qquad
\mathrm{E}[X^2]=\frac{0+2+12+36}{10}=5.
$$
Thus $\mathrm{Var}(X)=5-2^2=1$.

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="foundations probability pdf cdf" data-difficulty="1" #q-foundations-density-probability}
## Question 8: A density is not a point probability

A continuous random variable $X$ has CDF
$$
F_X(x)=
\begin{cases}
0,&x<0,\\
4x^2,&0\le x\le\tfrac12,\\
1,&x>\tfrac12.
\end{cases}
$$

(a) Find a probability density function for $X$ and check that it integrates
to one.  
(b) Find $\mathrm{Pr}(1/4<X\le1/2)$ and $\mathrm{Pr}(X=1/4)$.  
(c) Find $f_X(1/4)$. Is a density value greater than one a problem?  
(d) Find the median of $X$.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Differentiating the CDF on the interior of the support gives
$$
f_X(x)=8x\quad(0<x<1/2),
$$
with density zero outside this interval. Its values at the two endpoints may
be chosen arbitrarily without changing probabilities. It is non-negative and
$\int_0^{1/2}8x\,\mathrm{d}x=[4x^2]_0^{1/2}=1$.

**(b)** Probabilities come from CDF differences, or areas under the density:
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(1/4<X\le1/2)=F_X(1/2)-F_X(1/4)=1-\frac14=\frac34.
$$
There is no jump at $1/4$, so $\mathrm{Pr}(X=1/4)=0$. Changing an interval
endpoint from strict to non-strict makes no difference here.

**(c)** The density value is $f_X(1/4)=2$. This is allowed: a density is a
height, not a probability. Areas must lie between zero and one; individual
density values need not.

**(d)** Solve $F_X(m)=1/2$: $4m^2=1/2$, giving
$m=1/(2\sqrt2)\approx0.3536$. Half the probability lies on each side of this
value; the midpoint of the support need not be the median.

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="foundations probability joint-distribution conditional-probability independence expectation" data-difficulty="1" #q-foundations-joint-distribution}
## Question 9: Joint, marginal, and conditional probabilities

The joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y$ is given below. All other
pairs have probability zero.

| $X\backslash Y$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| $0$ | 0.10 | 0.20 | 0.10 |
| $1$ | 0.20 | 0.10 | 0.30 |

(a) Find both marginal PMFs.  
(b) Find $\mathrm{Pr}(X=1\mid Y=2)$.  
(c) Find the conditional PMF of $Y$ given $X=0$, and hence
$\mathrm{E}[Y\mid X=0]$.  
(d) Are $X$ and $Y$ independent?

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Row sums give $p_X(0)=0.40$ and $p_X(1)=0.60$. Column sums give
$p_Y(0)=0.30$, $p_Y(1)=0.30$, and $p_Y(2)=0.40$. Each marginal PMF sums to one.

**(b)** Restricting to the column $Y=2$,
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(X=1\mid Y=2)=\frac{p_{X,Y}(1,2)}{p_Y(2)}
=\frac{0.30}{0.40}=0.75.
$$

**(c)** Dividing the $X=0$ row by its total $0.40$ gives
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(Y=0\mid X=0)=0.25,\quad
\mathrm{Pr}(Y=1\mid X=0)=0.50,\quad
\mathrm{Pr}(Y=2\mid X=0)=0.25.
$$
Therefore $\mathrm{E}[Y\mid X=0]=0(0.25)+1(0.50)+2(0.25)=1$.
Using the original row without normalising would not give a conditional PMF.

**(d)** No. For example,
$$
p_{X,Y}(0,0)=0.10\ne(0.40)(0.30)=p_X(0)p_Y(0).
$$
Independence requires this factorisation for every pair; one counterexample
is enough to rule it out.

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="foundations probability expectation covariance correlation independence" data-difficulty="1" #q-foundations-uncorrelated-dependent}
## Question 10: Zero correlation does not imply independence

Let $X$ take the values $-1$, $0$, and $1$, each with probability $1/3$, and
define $Y=X^2$.

(a) Find $\mathrm{E}[X]$, $\mathrm{E}[Y]$, and $\mathrm{E}[XY]$.  
(b) Find the covariance and correlation of $X$ and $Y$. You may use
$\mathrm{Var}(X)=2/3$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Y)=2/9$.  
(c) Show that $X$ and $Y$ are nevertheless dependent.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Direct summation gives
$$
\mathrm{E}[X]=\frac{-1+0+1}{3}=0,\qquad
\mathrm{E}[Y]=\frac{1+0+1}{3}=\frac23.
$$
Since $XY=X^3$, $\mathrm{E}[XY]=(-1+0+1)/3=0$.

**(b)** Thus
$$
\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathrm{E}[XY]-\mathrm{E}[X]\mathrm{E}[Y]=0.
$$
Both variances are positive, so the correlation is defined and equals zero.

**(c)** If $X=0$, then $Y=0$ with certainty, whereas $\mathrm{Pr}(Y=0)=1/3$:
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(Y=0\mid X=0)=1\ne\mathrm{Pr}(Y=0).
$$
Zero correlation excludes a linear association as measured by covariance;
it does not exclude a nonlinear relationship such as $Y=X^2$.

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="foundations probability bernoulli expectation variance independence" data-difficulty="0" #q-foundations-indicators}
## Question 11: Counting events with indicator variables

Four components have fault probabilities $p_1=0.1$, $p_2=0.2$, $p_3=0.3$, and
$p_4=0.4$. Define $I_i=1$ if component $i$ is faulty and $I_i=0$ otherwise.
Let $N=I_1+I_2+I_3+I_4$ be the number of faulty components.

(a) Find $\mathrm{E}[N]$ without assuming independence.  
(b) Now assume the fault indicators are independent. Find $\mathrm{Var}(N)$.  
(c) Explain why $N$ is not Binomial with parameters $4$ and $0.25$, even though
the average fault probability is $0.25$.  
(d) Without independence, what additional information would be needed to find
$\mathrm{Var}(N)$?

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Each $I_i$ is Bernoulli with mean $p_i$. Linearity of expectation gives
$$
\mathrm{E}[N]=\sum_{i=1}^4p_i=1.
$$
This calculation does not need independence.

**(b)** Under independence, the covariances vanish, so
$$
\mathrm{Var}(N)=\sum_{i=1}^4p_i(1-p_i)
=0.09+0.16+0.21+0.24=0.70.
$$

**(c)** A Binomial model assumes a common success probability as well as
independent trials. Here the probabilities differ. In particular, a
$\mathrm{Binomial}(4,0.25)$ variable would have variance
$4(0.25)(0.75)=0.75$, which differs from part (b).

**(d)** The pairwise covariances, or equivalent joint fault probabilities, are
needed because in general
$$
\mathrm{Var}(N)=\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)+2\sum_{i<j}\mathrm{Cov}(I_i,I_j).
$$
The four marginal fault probabilities alone are insufficient.

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="foundations probability normal standard-error" data-difficulty="0" #q-foundations-normal-mean}
## Question 12: One observation versus a sample mean

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_{25}$ be independent $\mathcal N(50,100)$ measurements, where
the second Normal parameter is the **variance**. Let $\bar X$ be their mean.
You may use $\Phi(0.4)=0.6554$ and $\Phi(2)=0.9772$, where $\Phi$ is the
standard Normal CDF.

(a) State the standard deviations of $X_1$ and $\bar X$.  
(b) Find $\mathrm{Pr}(X_1>54)$ and $\mathrm{Pr}(\bar X>54)$.  
(c) Is the Normal distribution of $\bar X$ exact or a CLT approximation here?

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** One measurement has standard deviation $\sqrt{100}=10$. Independence
gives $\mathrm{Var}(\bar X)=100/25=4$, so the standard deviation of the mean
(its standard error) is $2$.

**(b)** Standardise with the standard deviation of the quantity in question:
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(X_1>54)=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{54-50}{10}\right)
=1-0.6554=0.3446,
$$
whereas
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(\bar X>54)=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{54-50}{2}\right)
=1-0.9772=0.0228.
$$
Averaging reduces variability, so the same distance above the mean is much
less likely for $\bar X$.

**(c)** It is exact: a linear combination of independent Normal random
variables is Normal, so $\bar X\sim\mathcal N(50,4)$. A large-sample
approximation is unnecessary under this model.

</details>

:::
